new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Word stress in Karakalpak is dynamic (expiratory) and, as a rule, falls on the last syllable. Phrasal stress is musical and serves for the logical highlighting of the semantically principal words.

Surrounding section: 2.1.0 Фонологические сведения; 2.1.1 nine vowels + vowel and consonant tables; 2.1.2 the stress paragraph; 2.1.3 vowel/consonant harmony (labial attraction limited to n…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word (as a rule); it is a dynamic/expiratory stress. Phrase-level prominence is described separately as pitch-based (musical) emphasis.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in Baskakov 1997. (Polivanov 1933 pp. 16-17 uses separate marks for main and secondary stress in his texts but states no rule.)
new_statements.exceptions: None in Baskakov 1997 beyond the hedge 'как правило' (as a rule). Polivanov 1933 (text notes, pp. 17-19) records 'displacement' of stress onto the first syllable in interrogative words (ne 'what?') and occasionally in polysyllables, i.e. non-final stress treated as marked deviation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('словесное ударение'), explicitly contrasted with phrasal stress ('ударение фразовое') in the same paragraph. Description is of literary Karakalpak, based on the north-eastern (northern) dialect (p. 264, 1.3.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Baskakov 1997 describes standard/literary Karakalpak, which is based on the north-eastern (northern) dialect (p. 264, 1.3.2); he notes two weakly differentiated dialects (NE close to Kazakh, SW close to Uzbek/Turkmen). Polivanov 1933 records the Qongrat (Kungrad) district speech. Both fall under kara1467; no separate Glottolog dialect codes asserted.
